editor.qualityPlainTranscode: The highs stop dead at {{cutoff}}, like an MP3. Converting it won't bring the quality back.
editor.qualityPlainBad: The highs stop dead at {{cutoff}}, the mark of a compressed file. Converting it won't bring the quality back.
editor.qualityPlainWarn: The highs only reach {{cutoff}}, short of a full master. It may come from a compressed file.
editor.qualityPlainProcessed: The highs above {{cutoff}} are made up to make it look complete. The source was compressed, and converting it won't fix that.
editor.qualityPlainUpsampled: It claims {{rate}}, but the audio is 44.1 kHz scaled up. It isn't real high resolution.
editor.qualityPlainPadded: It claims 24 bits, but it is 16-bit audio padded with zeros. It sounds no worse, it just takes more space.
editor.qualityCaptionGood: Energy reaches ~{{cutoff}}, at the ~20 kHz full-quality line.
editor.qualityCaptionWarn: Energy reaches ~{{cutoff}}, short of the ~20 kHz full-quality line.
editor.qualityCaptionBad: Ceiling at ~{{cutoff}}, the mark of a lossy source.
editor.qualityCaptionProcessed: Highs that rise where a natural spectrum falls — regenerated over a real ceiling near ~{{cutoff}}.
editor.qualityUpsampled: Declared above 44.1 kHz, but the real content walls off at 22.05 kHz — upsampled from 44.1 kHz, not true hi-res.
editor.qualityHiRes: Content really carries above 22.05 kHz, so the {{rate}} rate is doing real work rather than padding a 44.1 kHz source.
editor.qualityResolutionUnknown: The sample rate could not be verified: the probe above 22.05 kHz was unreadable, so this file is neither confirmed hi-res nor flagged as upsampled.
editor.qualityBitsPadded: Declared 24-bit, but the low 8 bits are zero in every sample: 16-bit audio padded into a 24-bit container.
editor.qualityBitsPaddedWhy: Interpolation, dither, any real 24-bit pipeline fills those bits; all-zero is arithmetic proof, not statistics.
editor.qualityBitsPaddedNote: Converting with bit depth “Corrected” writes true 16-bit; dropping the padding is lossless.
editor.qualityBitsFull: The declared 24-bit depth is real: {{pct}}% of samples use the lowest byte.
editor.qualityBitsUnknown: The declared 24-bit depth could not be verified: the scanned minute gave no clean reading either way.
editor.qualityConvertRateSub: Sample rate is set to “Corrected” and this file's wall is measured at 22.05 kHz, so the copy is written at the rate the audio really has. Nothing musical above it is lost.
editor.qualityCaptionGenuine: No codec cut: tapers smoothly to ~{{cutoff}}, a gently rolled-off but genuine master.
editor.qualityCaptionTranscode: A codec cut at ~{{cutoff}} inside a lossless container: the source was already lossy, even if the file itself is a faithful copy.
editor.qualityCaptionLossy: A codec cut at ~{{cutoff}}, normal for this format. Below ~19 kHz it points to a lower bitrate.
editor.qualityEvidenceGood: Energy reaches ~{{cutoff}} and the steepest fall across a kilohertz on the way is just {{drop}} dB: a fade, not a codec cliff, and no synthetic fill.
editor.qualityEvidenceTranscode: A codec cut at ~{{cutoff}} inside a lossless container: the energy drops {{drop}} dB within one kilohertz and stays down. The source was already lossy, even if the file is a faithful copy.
editor.qualityEvidenceLossy: A codec cut at ~{{cutoff}}: the energy drops {{drop}} dB within one kilohertz and stays down. Below ~19 kHz it points to a lower bitrate.
editor.qualityEvidenceWallWhy: A fade loses a few decibels per band; only an encoder falls off a cliff.
editor.qualityEvidenceTeeth: The fine bands rise {{teeth}} times between {{from}} and {{to}}, where a natural spectrum only falls: synthetic highs over a real ceiling near ~{{cutoff}}.
editor.qualityEvidenceTeethWhy: An enhancer's patches meet in a saw-tooth; real air never climbs back up.
editor.qualityEvidenceHump: The energy falls to a valley at ~{{cutoff}}, then rises to a crest near {{peak}}: highs that grow where a natural spectrum only falls.
editor.qualityEvidenceHumpWhy: An upscaler papers a synthetic hump over the old cutoff; the valley underneath is the true edge of the source.
editor.qualityEvidenceShelf: The top octave holds dead flat out to the edge, well under the body of the mix: synthetic fill over a real ceiling near ~{{cutoff}}.
editor.qualityEvidenceShelfWhy: Real highs wander and fade; only generated noise sits this flat.

editor.loudnessLufsHelp: (LUFS) — how loud the track sounds overall. Too low and it plays quieter than your other tracks; too high and it sounds crushed.
editor.loudnessPeakHelp: (dBTP) — the loudest instant of the signal. Above 0 it can distort (clip) when converted or played back.
editor.loudnessRangeHelp: (LU) — how much the quiet and loud parts differ. A very low range means heavy compression (the loudness war).
editor.loudnessCrestHelp: (dB) — the gap between the peaks and the average level, i.e. the punch. A low figure means the track is squashed flat.
editor.loudnessBalanceHelp: (L/R) — the level difference between the left and right channels. A few dB means one side is weaker, often a misaligned cartridge on the rip.
editor.loudnessDcHelp: — a constant bias that shifts the whole waveform off centre. It wastes headroom and can add clicks; near 0% is healthy.
editor.loudnessNoiseHelp: (dB) — the level of the background hiss/noise. The lower (more negative), the cleaner the capture.

token.q: Do I need a Discogs token?
token.a:
No. Surco searches Discogs out of the box using its own app credentials, so you can start tagging right away.

Those shared credentials have a combined rate limit (60 requests/minute across all Surco users), so during busy moments a search may occasionally fail with a “rate limit reached” message — just wait a few seconds and try again.

If you tag a lot, generate your own free personal token at discogs.com/settings/developers and paste it in Settings → Search. Your token gets its own private rate limit, so searches stay fast no matter how busy Surco is.

quality.q: Why is a track flagged as “Doubtful”?
quality.a:
Surco analyzes the audio spectrum and checks how high the frequencies reach. Genuine lossless files (WAV, FLAC, AIFF) use the full range up to the Nyquist frequency. A sharp cutoff well below it is the fingerprint of a lossy MP3 that was re-encoded into a lossless container: it looks lossless by its extension, but the high frequencies are gone for good.

“Doubtful” means that fingerprint was detected and is worth a listen: the file isn't broken, but its quality may be capped by an original MP3 (or it's simply a dull master). “Good quality” means the spectrum reaches where a real lossless file should.

format.q: Which output format should I choose?
format.a:
AIFF and WAV are lossless — they keep the exact original quality and carry tags cleanly, ideal for DJing. AIFF tends to handle metadata and artwork best on Apple platforms.

MP3 (320 kbps) is lossy but takes far less space — handy when storage or USB size matters.

Whichever you pick, a file already in that format is copied without re-encoding, so you never lose quality to a needless conversion.

appleMusic.q: What does “Add to Apple Music” do?
appleMusic.a:
When enabled (macOS only), Surco automatically imports each converted track into your Apple Music library right after converting it, so your freshly tagged files land there without a manual drag-and-drop.

While editing, Surco also checks whether a track is already in your library and shows a small badge, so you don't create duplicates. You can turn auto-add off anytime in Settings → Output.

windows.a:
Almost everything works exactly the same: conversion, tagging, Discogs, Bandcamp and Deezer search, quality analysis, and the rekordbox, Traktor, Serato and Engine DJ exports.

The one piece that doesn't exist on Windows is the Apple Music integration. Surco drives Apple's Music app through AppleScript, an automation bridge that only exists on macOS — the Apple Music app for Windows offers nothing equivalent — so the Apple Music destination, buttons and library badge simply don't appear.

One WAV quirk worth knowing: Surco stores WAV tags in the standard ID3 chunk, which DJ apps and tag editors like Mp3tag read fine, but Windows Explorer can't display — a converted WAV can look untagged in a folder even though every tag is there. With MP3 or FLAC, Explorer shows them normally.
